messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable, Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Evelyn was 68 years old, African American, married, and not working outside the home when she came for help, though she described herself as someone who had long kept herself useful by staying occupied. She spoke in a careful, measured way, with the manner of a woman who had learned to read a room quickly and keep her own feelings tucked away. The violence she linked her difficulties to had taken place years earlier, during a relationship in which her partner hurt her physically in private and left her feeling that even familiar spaces could become dangerous without warning. She did not linger on every detail at once; instead, the account came out in fragments, as though she had to approach it from the side. What stood out was how exposed she had felt in moments when she was alone with him, and how the experience had taught her to watch for shifts in mood, posture, and tone before anything happened. Even now, Evelyn said she felt most vulnerable when she was emotionally open with someone or when she was sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place, because those were the times her body seemed to remember that being unguarded had once come at a cost.

Over time, she had built her life around making herself easy to be around and hard to challenge. With family, neighbors, and even casual acquaintances, she described going along with whatever others wanted if it kept things calm. She would agree to plans she did not prefer, swallow objections, and make herself useful rather than risk tension. She spoke of this not as a theory but as a habit she depended on, something that made her feel safer in the moment. Alongside this, she kept herself busy with chores, errands, and small tasks around the house, and when her thoughts threatened to settle on what had happened, she tried to fill every gap in her day. She also kept her mind occupied all the time, deliberately turning to practical concerns, television, or routine activities whenever quiet allowed her memory too much room. To Evelyn, stillness was not restful; it was the condition in which the past could get in.

Her symptoms had become especially noticeable at night. She said she had difficulty falling asleep because she needed to stay alert, and that sense of vigilance followed her even inside her own home. Although she and her husband shared a life together, she described only a limited number of places as feeling truly safe, and even then that safety felt fragile and specific, as if it depended on being in the right room, at the right time, with the right door locked. If she was in a bedroom that was not her own, or if she had to sleep somewhere unfamiliar, her body became tense and watchful. She would lie awake listening, checking the room, and waiting for a feeling she could not fully name but knew well enough to fear. At home, too, she found herself on guard, scanning her surroundings before settling, as though danger could still step into the house.

The memory of the abuse did not stay where she left it. Evelyn described it as something that forced its way into her mind when she did not want it to, arriving with no invitation and no concern for whether she was ready. At other times she found herself pushing it away before she could fully recall it, stopping short of the worst part because the full image felt too close, too vivid, and too hard to sit with. She also noted that something in her surroundings could bring the whole memory back without warning. One of the clearest examples she gave was the smell of soil and the outdoors. If she was outside tending to a yard, walking near freshly turned earth, or simply catching that damp, outdoor scent after rain, she could be swept back into the old fear before she had time to prepare. The smell did not just remind her in an abstract way; it seemed to open the door to the whole scene at once, making the past feel immediate and bodily.

Because of this, everyday life had narrowed in ways that surprised even her. She went through the motions of daily responsibilities, but she did so with a continuous effort to stay ahead of her own thoughts and reactions. Certain places and situations felt manageable only if she could keep control of her attention and her surroundings. She had become wary of being emotionally exposed, wary of sleeping in unfamiliar settings, and wary of the outdoor smells that could strike without warning. What finally brought her to treatment was the accumulation of all this vigilance and effort; she was tired of arranging her life around the possibility of being startled back into the memory. Evelyn hoped for relief, but she was also afraid that if she let her guard down, the old sense of danger would return with the same force as before.
